statements.quote: Before we can understand a Neural Network, we have to understand the language it speaks: **mathematics**.
This first of three math chapters covers the numerical foundations, the symbols and operations that appear constantly in AI code.
Long before anyone wrote a numeral, people counted by making marks.

The **Lebombo bone**, a baboon fibula from Border Cave, carries a row of incised notches and is dated to roughly 42,000–43,000 years ago by 24 radiocarbon measurements; it is plausibly a tally stick, though that reading is not certain (\cite[Bruderer, 2024]{lebombobone}).

The **Ishango bone** from the Congo, about 20,000 years old, has 168 marks arranged in three columns; proposed readings range from a base-12 counting aid to a lunar calendar (\cite[de Heinzelin, 1957]{ishangobone}; \cite[Pletser, 2012]{ishango12}).
Neither bone proves arithmetic, but both externalise number as a spatial pattern — the move every array, tensor and embedding still makes.
The first **place-value** systems grew out of accounting, not pure mathematics.

Sumerian scribes were counting in base 60 before 3500 BCE, and the Old Babylonians turned that inheritance into a positional sexagesimal system around 2000 BCE, using just two wedge symbols for the digits 1–59 (\cite[MacTutor: Babylonian Mathematics]{macTutorBabylonianMathematics}; \cite[MacTutor: Babylonian Numerals]{macTutorBabylonianNumerals}).
Egypt went the other way: its hieroglyphs were decimal but **not** positional, with separate signs for 1, 10, 100 and so on, and the Rhind Papyrus (c.
1650 BCE) works in unit fractions (\cite[MacTutor: Egyptian Numerals]{macTutorEgyptianNumerals}; \cite[Ahmes, c.
1650 BCE]{rhindpapyrus}).
In classical programming, you need to write every single step that has to be done with data.
This initializes a *variable* called $ x $, calculates the value of $ 1 + 1 $ and sets $ x $ to it.
*Variables* can be thought of as containers for values which you can use instead of concrete values.
You can also use more variables, like the next example uses $ y $, which, in turn, uses the value of $ x $ to print $ 3 $ after calculating its values.
Let's now introduce **functions**.
A function is something that accepts inputs and calculates an output, where the rules are specified from how to get from the inputs to the outputs.
Functions are useful, as they model reality.
You can see how the parameters affect the plot by changing them with the sliders:
We can use this $\text{add}$ function in the code, similar to what we had before.
We can also use other functions, like $\sin$ (the sine) in our functions, and we can also parameterize them to get more complex patterns:
Sets do not need to contain only numbers, though.
Sets can contain sets, or sets can contain images, or people, or whatever else that can be listed.
The *set* of jobs could be something like this: $\left\{\text{programmer}, \text{janitor}, \text{cashier}, \dots\right\}$.
Sets can have a limited number of elements (and even be empty), or have an unlimited amount of elements, like the set of all numbers.
Since, for each number, there's always a larger number, the set never ends.

There are certain sets that are useful to know, like $\mathbb{N}$, which is the set of all natural numbers, or $\mathbb{R}$, which is the set of all real numbers (i.e. all numbers we use in every day life when not simply counting, e.g. $1.8$ or $3.14$, but also every number from $\mathbb{N}$, or the set of so-called **boolean values** $\mathbb{B} = \left\{\text{True}, \text{False}\right\}$, but a set does not need to be any of them.
A function defines a rule such that, for each element of a set, applying that rule yields an element of another (or the same) set.
Some books define the natural numbers as $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$ (excluding $0$).
Both conventions are common.
Throughout this course we use the inclusive convention $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$, matching the convention most programming languages (and most AI libraries) use.
Zero entered mathematics twice, and the two entries are easy to confuse.

Babylonian scribes used a pair of wedges as an **empty-place marker** from about 400 BCE, but they did not treat it as a number, and they did not use it at the right-hand end of a numeral (\cite[MacTutor: A History of Zero]{macTutorZero}).

The decisive step is Brahmagupta's *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta* (628 CE), which gives rules for calculating with zero and negatives; his rule for a finite number divided by zero survives in Colebrooke's translation as "A definite quantity divided by cipher, is the submultiple of nought" (\cite[Colebrooke trans., 1817]{brahmagupta_colebrooke}).
Negative numbers appear first as **bookkeeping**, not as abstract objects.

The Chinese *Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*, compiled in the Han dynasty, uses positive and negative quantities in systems of linear equations, and Liu Hui (3rd century CE) states rules for adding and subtracting them (\cite[Han-dynasty compilers, 1st c.

Brahmagupta then gives the rule in words that still sound modern: "the difference of an affirmative and a negative quantity is their addition" (\cite[Colebrooke trans., 1817]{brahmagupta_colebrooke}).
The discovery that a square's diagonal is **incommensurable** with its side broke the Pythagorean programme that "all is number".
The proof is traditionally attributed to Hippasus (5th century BCE); Theodorus of Cyrene extended it to surds up to √17, and Eudoxus of Cnidus (c.
408–355 BCE) rebuilt proportion so that incommensurable magnitudes could be handled without pretending they were ratios of integers (\cite[MacTutor: Real Numbers]{macTutorRealNumbers}).
Euclid's *Elements* Book X organises the result (\cite{euclidelements}).
Only in 1872 did Dedekind give the modern definition: an irrational is a **cut** in the rationals (\cite[Dedekind, 1872]{dedekind1872}).

Cantor's 1895 definition is the source of the modern notation: "Unter einer 'Menge' verstehen wir jede Zusammenfassung M von bestimmten wohlunterschiedenen Objecten m unsrer Anschauung oder unseres Denkens ...
zu einem Ganzen" — a set is any collection of definite, distinct objects of our intuition or thought into a whole (\cite[Cantor, 1895]{cantor1895}).
The symbol $\in$ is younger: Peano introduced it in 1889, taking the first letter of the Greek *esti* ("is") (\cite[MacTutor: Set Theory]{macTutorSetTheory}).
Cantor's unrestricted "any collection" later forced axiomatisation after Russell's paradox (discovered around 1901–02) (\cite[MacTutor: Set Theory]{macTutorSetTheory}).
> **The number line was not given; it was built.** Tally marks (c.
42,000 BP) externalised counting; Babylon added place-value (c.
2000 BCE); Brahmagupta made zero a number (628 CE); Dedekind made the irrationals rigorous (1872).
Each step turned a practical trick into an object mathematics could calculate with.
In classical programming, you would specify each step by hand to define a function, but for some functions, this is barely possible since the problem is ill-defined or way too complex.
For example, imagine you need a program to tell images of cats and dogs apart.
You cannot simply write a function that checks for every single pixel value, because then you'd need to know every single possible image of a cat or a dog, which is an infinite amount.
This is where AI comes in.
AI replaces the idea of a hand-written *function* with a *model* that does what you want, and doesn't do it by a list of handwritten rules, but learns how to do it by example.
For example, you may have a large set of images of cats and dogs, and the information for each image, if it shows a cat or a dog.
Then, you'd have 2 sets, one, the set of all images, and the set of results like $\left\{\text{cat}, \text{dog}\right\}$, where each Image is mapped to one of those results, ie.
you know that you want $\text{function}\left(\text{Image of a cat}\right) \rightarrow \text{cat}$ and $\text{function}\left(\text{Image of a dog}\right) \rightarrow \text{dog}$.
AI then learns how to get from that input to that output.
You only provide basic building blocks it should use, which depend on the type of task you want it to solve.
This model will (most probably) not be perfect.
But it can be **good enough** to be useful.
Throughout this course, we will look into these building blocks and how the computer then creates this model, and how these building blocks work.

We'll start with very simple building blocks for simple numbers, and then go to building blocks to classify images, and end up with Transformers, which are the basic structure for chatGPT, which all take ideas from each other.

The idea of summing infinite series to achieve finite results dates back to antiquity, notably Zeno's paradox, later addressed through Archimedes's method of exhaustion.

The reason $2^{0.5}$ (or $2^{1/2}$) equals $\sqrt{2}$ comes from the fundamental rule of exponents: when you multiply two powers with the same base, you add the exponents (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch.
If we multiply $2^{0.5}$ by itself, the rule says:

Negative exponents do not mean the result becomes negative; instead, they represent the **reciprocal** (division) (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch.
A negative exponent tells you to “divide” instead of “multiply.”
In the context of the continuous curve, as the exponent moves into negative territory, the result simply gets closer and closer to zero, but never quite touches it.
This is why logarithms (the inverse) are so useful, they allow us to work with these tiny, microscopic fractions by looking at the exponent instead of the decimal.
For example, if we ask “To what power must we raise 2 to get 8?” ($\log_2(8) = ?$), the answer is 3.
Abstractly, a logarithm transforms a scale of growth (multiplicative) into a scale of steps (additive) (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch.

It tells you the “size” or “order of magnitude” of a number rather than just its value.

Jost Bürgi reached logarithms independently around 1588 and published them in 1620; Kepler wrote that Bürgi had them "many years before Napier's system appeared" (\cite[MacTutor: Jost Bürgi]{macTutorBurgi}).
Kepler's *Chilias logarithmorum* (1624) supplied the first proof of why the method works, based on Euclid's Book V (\cite[Kepler, 1624]{kepler1624chilias}).
Napier's breakthrough allowed researchers to perform **multiplication by simply adding**:
By using “Log Tables,” an astronomer could look up the logarithms of two giant numbers, add them, and then find the corresponding “anti-logarithm” to get the product.

This revolutionary efficiency led the mathematician \citeauthor{laplace1821} to write in \citeyear{laplace1821} that logarithms were *“an admirable artifice which, by reducing to a few days the labour of many months, doubles the life of the astronomer”* (p.
Historically, one of the most fundamental tools is the **Mercator series** \citealternativetitle{mercator1668} (p.
32f) for the natural logarithm ($\ln$):
This is the series that taught mathematicians to think of $\ln$ as a limit of polynomials.
Modern floating-point units, however, do not evaluate it term-by-term in the hot path — the alternating series converges slowly and accumulates rounding error badly.

Instead, math libraries reduce the problem to a small interval (e.g., $\ln(x) = \ln(x/2^k) + k\ln 2$), then approximate on that interval with a **rational function** (a Padé / Remez minimax polynomial), a **CORDIC** iteration in hardware, or a short **table lookup with interpolation**.
The Mercator series is the historical and didactic root; the polynomial a CPU actually evaluates on a single call is much shorter, of higher degree, and tuned for the working interval.
While logarithms were born from the needs of 17th-century astronomers, they are essential for Artificial Intelligence today.
In neural networks, we use them to prevent numerical errors when dealing with tiny probabilities and to calculate how “wrong” a model is during training.

Zero entered mathematics twice, and the two entries are easy to confuse. Babylonian scribes used a pair of wedges as an **empty-place marker** from about 400 BCE, but they did not treat it as a number, and they did not use it at the right-hand end of a numeral (\cite[MacTutor: A History of Zero]{macTutorZero}). The decisive step is Brahmagupta's *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta* (628 CE), which gives rules for calculating with zero and negatives; his rule for a finite number divided by zero survives in Colebrooke's translation as "A definite quantity divided by cipher, is the submultiple of nought" (\cite[Colebrooke trans., 1817]{brahmagupta_colebrooke}).

Negative numbers appear first as **bookkeeping**, not as abstract objects. The Chinese *Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*, compiled in the Han dynasty, uses positive and negative quantities in systems of linear equations, and Liu Hui (3rd century CE) states rules for adding and subtracting them (\cite[Han-dynasty compilers, 1st c. BCE]{jiuzhangsuanshu}). Brahmagupta then gives the rule in words that still sound modern: "the difference of an affirmative and a negative quantity is their addition" (\cite[Colebrooke trans., 1817]{brahmagupta_colebrooke}).

The discovery that a square's diagonal is **incommensurable** with its side broke the Pythagorean programme that "all is number". The proof is traditionally attributed to Hippasus (5th century BCE); Theodorus of Cyrene extended it to surds up to √17, and Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 408–355 BCE) rebuilt proportion so that incommensurable magnitudes could be handled without pretending they were ratios of integers (\cite[MacTutor: Real Numbers]{macTutorRealNumbers}). Euclid's *Elements* Book X organises the result (\cite{euclidelements}). Only in 1872 did Dedekind give the modern definition: an irrational is a **cut** in the rationals (\cite[Dedekind, 1872]{dedekind1872}).

Cantor's 1895 definition is the source of the modern notation: "Unter einer 'Menge' verstehen wir jede Zusammenfassung M von bestimmten wohlunterschiedenen Objecten m unsrer Anschauung oder unseres Denkens ... zu einem Ganzen" — a set is any collection of definite, distinct objects of our intuition or thought into a whole (\cite[Cantor, 1895]{cantor1895}). The symbol $\in$ is younger: Peano introduced it in 1889, taking the first letter of the Greek *esti* ("is") (\cite[MacTutor: Set Theory]{macTutorSetTheory}). Cantor's unrestricted "any collection" later forced axiomatisation after Russell's paradox (discovered around 1901–02) (\cite[MacTutor: Set Theory]{macTutorSetTheory}).

> **The number line was not given; it was built.** Tally marks (c. 42,000 BP) externalised counting; Babylon added place-value (c. 2000 BCE); Brahmagupta made zero a number (628 CE); Dedekind made the irrationals rigorous (1872). Each step turned a practical trick into an object mathematics could calculate with.
Classical programming vs. AI
In classical programming, you would specify each step by hand to define a function, but for some functions, this is barely possible since the problem is ill-defined or way too complex.

For example, imagine you need a program to tell images of cats and dogs apart. Where do you start? You cannot simply write a function that checks for every single pixel value, because then you'd need to know every single possible image of a cat or a dog, which is an infinite amount.

This is where AI comes in. AI replaces the idea of a hand-written *function* with a *model* that does what you want, and doesn't do it by a list of handwritten rules, but learns how to do it by example. For example, you may have a large set of images of cats and dogs, and the information for each image, if it shows a cat or a dog. Then, you'd have 2 sets, one, the set of all images, and the set of results like $\left\{\text{cat}, \text{dog}\right\}$, where each Image is mapped to one of those results, ie. you know that you want $\text{function}\left(\text{Image of a cat}\right) \rightarrow \text{cat}$ and $\text{function}\left(\text{Image of a dog}\right) \rightarrow \text{dog}$. AI then learns how to get from that input to that output. You only provide basic building blocks it should use, which depend on the type of task you want it to solve.
This model will (most probably) not be perfect. But it can be **good enough** to be useful.

Throughout this course, we will look into these building blocks and how the computer then creates this model, and how these building blocks work. We'll start with very simple building blocks for simple numbers, and then go to building blocks to classify images, and end up with Transformers, which are the basic structure for chatGPT, which all take ideas from each other.

Arithmetic with $\infty$ in Computing
In the floating-point math used by AI models, infinity follows specific rules that allow the model to simplify complex logic:

Any finite number divided by infinity approaches zero. This is crucial for normalization, helping the model turn massive raw scores into manageable probabilities. The exponential of negative infinity is exactly zero. This is useful in machine learning: it lets us “mask” certain pieces of data by assigning them a value of $-\infty$, which makes them effectively ignored. This becomes important later in the chapter on Transformers.
The Concept of Limits ($\lim$)
In computing, we treat $\infty$ as a value, but in mathematics, we use limits to describe behavior.
Exponentials and logarithms
Imagine you have 1.00 Euro in a bank that gives you 100% interest per year.

The idea of summing infinite series to achieve finite results dates back to antiquity, notably Zeno's paradox, later addressed through Archimedes's method of exhaustion. In the 14th century, the Indian mathematician Madhava of Sangamagrama gave the earliest known examples of specific Taylor series, for sine, cosine, and arctangent, though not the general method. His followers in the Kerala school, recorded in works such as the \citetitle{madhava}, developed further expansions over the following two centuries.

In early 1671, James Gregory independently discovered something like the general Maclaurin series (see \citetitle{gregoryachievements}), but never published his method, believing he had merely rediscovered work by Isaac Newton. In 1691–1692, Newton wrote down an explicit general formulation in an unpublished draft of \citetitle{newtonquadratura}, but the relevant sections were omitted from the 1704 publication.

It was not until 1715 that \citeauthor{taylor1715} published the first general method for constructing these series (pp. 21–23), after whom they are now named. The special case centered at zero was later named after \citeauthor{maclaurin}, who published the relevant work in 1742.
Exponentiation
In its simplest form, exponentiation is repeated multiplication (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch. 1, §3, p. 18]{lang2005basicmath}). If we ask, “What is 2 to the power of 3?” ($2^3$), we mean:

The reason $2^{0.5}$ (or $2^{1/2}$) equals $\sqrt{2}$ comes from the fundamental rule of exponents: when you multiply two powers with the same base, you add the exponents (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch. 1, §3, p. 18]{lang2005basicmath}):
If we multiply $2^{0.5}$ by itself, the rule says:

Since $2^{0.5}$ is a number that, when multiplied by itself, results in $2$, it fits the literal definition of a square root. This logic extends to any floating-point number; for instance, $2^{0.333}$ is approximately the cube root ($\sqrt[3]{2}$) because adding $0.333 + 0.333 + 0.333$ brings us back to roughly $2^1$.

Negative exponents do not mean the result becomes negative; instead, they represent the **reciprocal** (division) (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch. 3, §3, p. 72]{lang2005basicmath}). A negative exponent tells you to “divide” instead of “multiply.”

In the context of the continuous curve, as the exponent moves into negative territory, the result simply gets closer and closer to zero, but never quite touches it. This is why logarithms (the inverse) are so useful, they allow us to work with these tiny, microscopic fractions by looking at the exponent instead of the decimal.
Logarithms: Reversing the Process
For example, if we ask “To what power must we raise 2 to get 8?” ($\log_2(8) = ?$), the answer is 3.

Abstractly, a logarithm transforms a scale of growth (multiplicative) into a scale of steps (additive) (\cite[Lang, Basic Mathematics, Ch. 13, §5, p. 339]{lang2005basicmath}). It tells you the “size” or “order of magnitude” of a number rather than just its value.
Logarithms were introduced in \citeyear{napier1614} by the Scottish mathematician John Napier in his landmark work \citealternativetitle{napier1614}.
\citealternativetitle{napier_portrait}.

Napier was not alone. Jost Bürgi reached logarithms independently around 1588 and published them in 1620; Kepler wrote that Bürgi had them "many years before Napier's system appeared" (\cite[MacTutor: Jost Bürgi]{macTutorBurgi}). Kepler's *Chilias logarithmorum* (1624) supplied the first proof of why the method works, based on Euclid's Book V (\cite[Kepler, 1624]{kepler1624chilias}).
Napier's breakthrough allowed researchers to perform **multiplication by simply adding**:

By using “Log Tables,” an astronomer could look up the logarithms of two giant numbers, add them, and then find the corresponding “anti-logarithm” to get the product. This revolutionary efficiency led the mathematician \citeauthor{laplace1821} to write in \citeyear{laplace1821} that logarithms were *“an admirable artifice which, by reducing to a few days the labour of many months, doubles the life of the astronomer”* (p. 96).
Historically, one of the most fundamental tools is the **Mercator series** \citealternativetitle{mercator1668} (p. 32f) for the natural logarithm ($\ln$):

This is the series that taught mathematicians to think of $\ln$ as a limit of polynomials. Modern floating-point units, however, do not evaluate it term-by-term in the hot path — the alternating series converges slowly and accumulates rounding error badly. Instead, math libraries reduce the problem to a small interval (e.g., $\ln(x) = \ln(x/2^k) + k\ln 2$), then approximate on that interval with a **rational function** (a Padé / Remez minimax polynomial), a **CORDIC** iteration in hardware, or a short **table lookup with interpolation**. The Mercator series is the historical and didactic root; the polynomial a CPU actually evaluates on a single call is much shorter, of higher degree, and tuned for the working interval.
The Change of Base

While logarithms were born from the needs of 17th-century astronomers, they are essential for Artificial Intelligence today. In neural networks, we use them to prevent numerical errors when dealing with tiny probabilities and to calculate how “wrong” a model is during training. We will dive deeper into “Log Loss” and “Softmax” in the upcoming sections.
The Mathematical Concept: The Role of $\infty$
blocks.section: The Mathematical Concept: The Role of $\infty$

blocks.quote: While we often view infinity as an endless loop or an impossibly large number, in the context of computer science and Large Language Models (LLMs), it acts as a functional tool. It allows systems to handle “impossible” states or “hidden” information without crashing the underlying logic. The use of the symbol $\infty$ for the concept of infinity dates back to \citeyear{wallis1655}, according to \citeauthor{historyofmathematicalnotation} (Vol. 1, p. 214).
blocks.section: The Mathematical Concept: The Role of $\infty$

blocks.quote: Wallis introduced the **symbol**, not the concept. Aristotle denied the **actual infinite** and allowed only the **potential infinite**: the natural numbers can always be extended, but never completed (*Physics* III.4–8) (\cite[MacTutor: Infinity]{macTutorInfinity}; \cite[Physics]{aristotlephysics}). Grosseteste's *De luce* (c. 1225) takes the opposite risk: light "multiplied itself by its very nature an infinite number of times on all sides", and "the multiplication of a simple being an infinite number of times must produce a finite quantity" (\cite[Grosseteste, trans. 1942]{grosseteste_on_light}). Wallis gave the concept its symbol: he introduced $\infty$ in 1655 and used it again in the *Arithmetica infinitorum* (1656) (\cite[Wallis, 1655]{wallis1655}; \cite[MacTutor: Infinity]{macTutorInfinity}).
blocks.section: The Mathematical Concept: The Role of $\infty$

blocks.quote: > **Potential, actual, symbolic.** Aristotle allowed only a potential infinite; Grosseteste argued that infinite multiplication produces a finite magnitude; Wallis gave the result its symbol, ∞ (1655). Mathematics kept all three ideas and learned to distinguish them.
